summary: Sets out requirements for a mechanism by which domains publish statements about their DKIM signing practices, separating must-have from highly desirable ones. It is informational.

eli5.summary: A list of what a mail sender's public rule should say, like whether all mail from a domain is signed.

subtitle: Requirements for publishing DKIM signing practices to help detect spoofed mail.

tldr.problem: DKIM signatures can prove a domain authorizes a message, but receivers cannot tell if a missing signature is expected or suspicious. Attackers can spoof unsigned mail from domains that actually sign everything.
tldr.mechanism: A domain publishes its DKIM signing practices—whether it signs all mail and what expectation receivers should have if a signature is missing or broken. Receivers use this to judge unsigned or damaged mail more harshly.
tldr.outcome: This RFC defines requirements for an SSP (Sender Signing Practices) protocol to help domains communicate their signing practices and let receivers treat unsigned mail with appropriate suspicion when a domain claims to sign everything.

facts.label: Deployment considerations
facts.value: 8 (outsourcing, subdomains, mailing lists, incremental roll-out, caching, legibility, extensibility, security)

facts.label: Key requirement
facts.value: Deterministic query answers in few message exchanges

today: RFC 5016 is an Informational requirements document. The DKIM Signing Practices specification was subsequently published as RFC 5617, which implements the requirements defined here.

sections.title: The DKIM Spoofing Problem
sections.content:
DomainKeys Identified Mail (DKIM) provides a cryptographic mechanism for domains to assert responsibility for messages they send. When a DKIM signature is present and valid, receivers can trust the domain's involvement. But when there is no signature, ambiguity arises: did the sender forget to sign, or did a forger send unsigned mail?

This ambiguity enables a trivial 'bid-down attack': an attacker simply sends unsigned mail from a domain. Since receivers do not know whether the domain signs everything or nothing, they cannot treat the lack of a signature as suspicious. A protocol to publish DKIM signing practices closes this gap.

Email is especially vulnerable because there is no a priori expectation of a domain's signing practices. Unlike established TLS certificates or public keys in a contact list, most email senders are unknown to most receivers.
sections.eli5: Without knowing if a company always signs its mail, you cannot tell if an unsigned email from that company is fake. A way to publish 'we sign everything' lets you spot fakes.

sections.title: Practices and Expectations
sections.content:
The RFC defines two key concepts: practice (a statement about externally verifiable behavior) and expectation (the likely survivability of the practice as a message traverses the internet). For example, a domain might publish that it sends 'DKIM Signing Complete' mail (all legitimate mail bears a valid first-party signature), but with uncertain expectation if the mail passes through mailing lists that might alter signatures.

The RFC distinguishes between first-party signatures (the domain's signature matches the From: address) and third-party signatures (other domains also signed the message). Requirements include the ability to publish both a practice (we sign all mail) and an expectation (we do not expect signatures to survive SMTP-modifying intermediaries versus we expect them to always survive).

Two problem scenarios are addressed: (1) a domain wants to signal that it signs all mail to warn receivers about unsigned mail that should be suspicious, and (2) a domain wants to signal a strong expectation that high-value mail (like banking) should always arrive signed, so missing signatures indicate a serious problem.
sections.eli5: A company says 'we sign everything' (practice) but might not expect that signature to survive if it goes through a mailing list (expectation). A bank might say 'our emails must always be signed' (strong expectation).

sections.title: Protocol Requirements
sections.content:
Discovery requirements specify that practices must be associated with the author's domain and published subordinate to it, answering queries with a small deterministic number of message exchanges (essentially prohibiting loops and extended delays). Publishing must not create ambiguity between different protocols' records at the same location.

Transport requirements demand existing widespread deployment (like DNS), low latency (fewer than three message exchanges), caching support for performance, and support for geographically diverse servers for high availability. The RFC recommends DNS as the transport mechanism because of its universal deployment and caching infrastructure.

Practice and expectation requirements include the ability to make assertions about the From: domain, precisely define first-party signatures, publish 'DKIM Signing Complete' status, and express high-expectation (messages must always be signed). Importantly, practices MUST be presented as information for local policy, not mandatory disposition instructions. Subdomains should inherit parent domain practices unless overridden.
sections.eli5: The protocol needs to be quick (like DNS), let domains publish simple statements like 'p=all' (we sign everything), and let receivers decide what to do with unsigned mail—not force a specific action.

sections.title: Deployment Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC addresses eight deployment scenarios. Outsourced signing requires domains to delegate signing to third parties (e.g., an ISP signs on behalf of a small business). Subdomain coverage protects parent domains from attacks on unspecified subdomains. Resent mail (forwarded by mailing lists) requires tracking which signatures survived.

Incremental deployment allows domains to gradually roll out signing. Performance and caching are critical because high-volume domains contact many others, and low-volume domains may be spoofing vectors. Human legibility ensures administrators can read and understand published practices.

Extensibility suggests the protocol should support future extensions beyond DKIM. Security requires robustness against DoS attacks and amplification attacks, with a path to strong source authentication (via DNSSEC).
sections.eli5: Small companies need to delegate to ISPs, mailing lists mess with signatures, not every domain rolls out signing at once. The protocol must be fast, human-readable, and safe from attacks.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
The RFC notes that SSP for high-value domains is a DoS target: if SSP records become unavailable, unsigned mail appears less suspicious. The protocol MUST prevent amplification attacks and maintain constant work complexity. It SHOULD enable DNSSEC signing for strong source authentication, though simpler unsigned publication is acceptable as a deployment compromise.

The RFC recommends using DNS as the transport mechanism, subject to threats described in RFC 4686 (threats to DKIM itself). DNSSEC is the natural path to authenticated SSP publication.
sections.eli5: An attacker might target the SSP service itself to hide spoofed mail. The protocol must not be exploitable for amplification attacks, and DNSSEC can prove SSP records are authentic.
